lessons.title: Forging a Basic Chisel from Coil Spring
lessons.body:
Coil springs from old cars or trucks are excellent sources of high-carbon steel, often 5160 or similar. Find a coil spring at a scrapyard or mechanic's shop. Use an angle grinder to cut one coil free, then heat it in your forge until it's bright orange (about 900Â°C). Straighten it with your hammer on the anvil. Cut a piece about 15 cm long. This will be your chisel.

Hold the steel with tongs and bring it to a bright yellow heat (1000-1100Â°C). Hammer one end into a flat, tapered edge. Work on both sides to create a symmetrical cutting edge. The edge should be about 2-3 mm thick at the tip and widen gradually to the body. Use a cross-peen hammer to draw out the metal. Keep the forging temperature high; if it turns dark red, stop and reheat.

Once the shape is formed, use a file or grinder to refine the cutting edge. For a wood chisel, a 25-degree bevel is good; for metal, 30-40 degrees. Then heat treat: heat the cutting end to non-magnetic (about 780Â°C), quench in warm oil (canola or motor oil). Test with a file; it should skate. Temper by heating the back of the chisel until the cutting edge turns straw yellow (230Â°C), then cool. Finally, sharpen on a stone.

Handle: you can leave it bare or add a wooden handle. For a bare chisel, round the struck end to prevent mushrooming. Always wear safety glasses and gloves. This chisel will cut hot metal, wood, or cold metal if tempered properly. In Africa, coil springs are plentiful and cheap, making this a sustainable tool-making method.

lessons.title: Creating a Punch from Tool Steel
lessons.body:
Tool steel like O1, W1, or even old files and ball bearings can be used to make a punch. If using a file, anneal it first: heat to 800Â°C and cool slowly in ash or vermiculite. This softens it for shaping. Cut a piece about 12-15 cm long and 1-2 cm thick. For a punch, you want a tapered point that will create holes in hot metal.

Heat the steel to bright orange and hammer one end into a taper. The point should be slightly rounded, not sharp, to avoid cracking. The taper should be gradual, about 5-7 cm long, ending in a tip of 2-3 mm diameter. Use a hammer and anvil to forge it. Keep the body straight. If you have a hardy hole, you can use a bolster to shape the taper. Reheat as needed. Once shaped, let it cool slowly.

Grind or file the tip to smooth it. Then heat treat: heat the tip to non-magnetic (780Â°C), quench in oil. Temper the tip to a light straw color (230Â°C) by heating the body until the tip changes color, then cool. This gives a hard tip with a tough body. For a hot punch, you might temper to a slightly higher temperature (purple, 280Â°C) to avoid cracking in hot metal.

Use your punch to make holes in hot metal for rivets, tongs, or decorative work. Always punch on a heavy anvil or a block of steel. Strike the punch with a heavy hammer. In Africa, old car axles and leaf springs are good sources of tool steel. This punch will last many years if properly heat treated.

lessons.title: Making Tongs from Flat Bar
lessons.body:
Tongs are essential for holding hot metal. You can make a simple pair from 1/2 inch (12 mm) flat bar, about 60 cm long. You'll need two pieces. Start by forging the jaws: heat one end of each bar to orange and hammer it into a tapered, slightly curved shape. The jaws should be about 10 cm long and curve inward to grip round or square stock. Use a cross-peen hammer to draw out the metal.

Next, forge the pivot boss. About 15 cm from the jaw end, upset the metal to create a thicker section. This will be the hinge. Heat that area and hammer it to make it wider and thicker. Then punch or drill a hole through both pieces at that point. The hole should be about 6-8 mm diameter. If you punch, do it hot and use a drift to size the hole.

Rivet the two pieces together with a piece of round bar (6 mm) or a bolt. Peen the rivet ends to secure. The tongs should open and close smoothly. Now forge the handles: draw out the remaining length to about 1 cm thick and 30 cm long. Curve the handles outward slightly so they don't pinch your hand. You can also forge a loop at the end for hanging.

Test the tongs on a piece of hot metal. Adjust the jaws by heating and bending if needed. The jaws should grip securely without wobbling. For different stock sizes, you can make multiple tongs or adjust the jaws. In Africa, flat bar is readily available at hardware stores. This project teaches you basic forging, punching, and riveting. With practice, you can make tongs in about two hours.

lessons.title: Forging a Hardy Tool for the Anvil
lessons.body:
A hardy tool is a shank that fits in the hardy hole of your anvil, used for cutting, fullering, or bending. Start with a piece of square bar that fits your anvil's hardy hole. Measure the hole: typically 2-3 cm square. Cut a piece of mild steel or tool steel about 15 cm long. One end will be the shank, the other the tool.

For a hot cut hardy, forge the top into a sharp, chisel-like edge. Heat the steel to orange and hammer the end into a wedge shape. The edge should be about 5 cm wide and taper to a sharp edge. Keep the shank square and slightly tapered so it wedges into the hole. You can also make a fuller hardy by forging a rounded edge, or a bending fork by cutting two prongs.

Heat treat the cutting edge if using tool steel: heat to non-magnetic, quench in oil, temper to straw. For mild steel, it won't harden much, but it's fine for hot cutting. The shank should be a loose fit; don't force it. File the shank to fit if needed.

To use, drop the shank into the hardy hole. The tool should sit securely. For cutting, place hot metal on the edge and strike with a hammer. The hardy takes the place of a chisel, leaving your hands free. Always wear safety glasses. In Africa, you can make a hardy from an old axle or leaf spring. This tool expands your anvil's versatility and is a great beginner project.

lessons.title: Heat Treating Your Homemade Tools
lessons.body:
Heat treating hardens and tempers steel so it holds an edge without being brittle. You need a forge, oil quench tank, and a way to measure temperature. If you don't have a thermometer, learn to judge by color: non-magnetic is about 780Â°C (bright red). Heat your tool's cutting edge to that temperature. Use a magnet to test; when it stops sticking, it's ready.

Quench immediately in warm oil (about 50-60Â°C). Canola, peanut, or motor oil works. Vegetable oil is common in Africa. Submerge the tool vertically, edge first, and move it around to cool quickly. Don't use water for most tool steels; it can crack them. After quenching, the steel is hard and brittle. Test with a file: it should skate without cutting.

Now temper: this reduces brittleness. Clean the steel to bare metal. Heat the tool away from the edge, letting heat travel to the edge. Watch for oxide colors: straw (230Â°C) for cutting tools, brown (260Â°C) for punches, purple (280Â°C) for springs. When the edge reaches the desired color, quench in oil to stop the process. Alternatively, use an oven at 200-250Â°C for one hour.

Always temper after hardening. Test your tool on scrap metal. If it chips, temper more; if it bends, harden again. Practice on scrap pieces first. In Africa, you can use a charcoal forge and a metal bucket for quench oil. Heat treating is the difference between a tool that works and one that fails. Take your time and be consistent.

lessons.title: Testing and Refining Your Tools
lessons.body:
After making and heat treating your tools, test them on actual work. For a chisel, try cutting cold mild steel or hot metal. It should cut without chipping or rolling. If the edge rolls, it's too soft; re-harden and temper to a lower temperature. If it chips, it's too hard; temper to a higher temperature. For a punch, punch a hole in hot metal; the tip should not deform.

For tongs, test grip on various stock sizes. If the jaws don't hold, heat and adjust the curve. The rivet should allow smooth movement but not be too loose. For a hardy, ensure it fits snugly but can be removed. Test cutting hot metal; the edge should stay sharp.

Refining: use a grinder or file to sharpen edges. For chisels, maintain a bevel angle of 25-30 degrees. For punches, keep the tip slightly rounded. Dress the striking end of tools to remove mushrooming. Always wear safety glasses when testing; pieces can fly.

Keep a log of your heat treating colors and results. Adjust as needed. In Africa, you can test on local materials like hardwood or scrap metal. Share your tools with other smiths for feedback. A well-made tool lasts years. If a tool fails, don't discard it; reforge and re-treat. Practice makes perfect. Your skills will improve with each tool you make.

quiz.q: What type of steel is commonly found in coil springs?
quiz.explanation: Coil springs are typically made from 5160 or similar high-carbon steel, which is ideal for tools.

quiz.q: At what temperature should you forge coil spring steel?
quiz.explanation: Forging is best done at bright orange to yellow heat, around 900-1100Â°C, for proper shaping.

quiz.q: What is the ideal bevel angle for a wood chisel?
quiz.explanation: A 25-degree bevel is standard for wood chisels to balance sharpness and durability.

quiz.q: How do you test if steel is ready for quenching?
options: B) A magnet sticks to it
C) A magnet does not stick
quiz.explanation: Steel becomes non-magnetic at around 780Â°C, which is the correct temperature for hardening.

quiz.q: What color should a chisel edge be tempered to?
quiz.explanation: Straw yellow (230Â°C) is the correct tempering color for cutting tools like chisels.

quiz.q: What is the first step when making a punch from an old file?
quiz.explanation: Old files are hard and brittle; annealing softens them for shaping.

quiz.q: What shape should the tip of a punch be?
quiz.explanation: A slightly rounded tip prevents cracking and creates cleaner holes.

quiz.q: What is the ideal tempering color for a hot punch?
quiz.explanation: Purple (280Â°C) provides a tougher temper suitable for hot punching.

quiz.q: What material is commonly used to make tongs in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: 1/2 inch (12 mm) flat bar is readily available and suitable for forging tongs.

quiz.q: How far from the jaw end should the pivot boss be?
quiz.explanation: The pivot boss is typically about 15 cm from the jaw end to allow proper leverage.

quiz.q: What is used to rivet the tongs together?
options: B) A piece of round bar or bolt
quiz.explanation: A 6 mm round bar or bolt makes a sturdy rivet for the tong pivot.

quiz.q: Why should tong handles be curved outward?
quiz.explanation: Curving handles outward prevents them from pinching your hand when gripping hot metal.

quiz.q: What is a hardy tool used for?
quiz.explanation: A hardy tool fits in the anvil's hardy hole and is used for various shaping tasks.

quiz.q: How should the shank of a hardy tool fit the hardy hole?
quiz.explanation: A loose fit allows easy insertion and removal; it should not be forced.

quiz.q: What can you use to make a hardy tool if tool steel is unavailable?
quiz.explanation: Mild steel works for hot cutting hardies, though it won't harden as much.

quiz.q: What is the correct quenching medium for most tool steels?
quiz.explanation: Warm oil (50-60Â°C) is recommended to avoid cracking and achieve proper hardness.

quiz.q: What color indicates non-magnetic temperature for hardening?
quiz.explanation: Non-magnetic occurs at about 780Â°C, which is a bright red color.

quiz.q: What does tempering do to steel?
options: B) Softens it slightly to reduce brittleness
quiz.explanation: Tempering reduces brittleness while maintaining most of the hardness.

quiz.q: What is the tempering color for a spring?
quiz.explanation: Blue (around 300Â°C) is the tempering color for springs, providing toughness.

quiz.q: How can you test if a chisel is properly hardened?
options: A) Hit it with a hammer
quiz.explanation: A file should skate over a properly hardened edge without cutting.

quiz.q: What should you do if a chisel edge rolls during use?
options: A) Temper to a higher temperature
B) Re-harden and temper to a lower temperature
quiz.explanation: Rolling indicates the edge is too soft; re-harden and temper to a lower temperature for more hardness.

quiz.q: What should you do if a chisel chips during use?
options: A) Temper to a higher temperature
B) Re-harden and temper to a lower temperature
quiz.explanation: Chipping means the edge is too hard; temper to a higher temperature to increase toughness.

quiz.q: What is a good way to refine the jaws of tongs?
quiz.explanation: Heating and bending allows you to adjust the jaws for a better grip.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a log of heat treating colors?
options: B) To track and improve results
quiz.explanation: A log helps you consistently reproduce successful heat treatments.

quiz.q: What safety gear should you wear when testing tools?
quiz.explanation: Always wear safety glasses, gloves, and an apron to protect from flying pieces and heat.

quiz.q: What is the ideal forging temperature for tool steel?
quiz.explanation: Tool steel is best forged at around 1000Â°C (bright yellow) for good movement.

quiz.q: How long should you temper a tool in an oven?
quiz.explanation: Tempering in an oven at 200-250Â°C for one hour is a common practice.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a hardy tool's shank?
options: B) To fit in the hardy hole
quiz.explanation: The shank fits into the anvil's hardy hole to secure the tool.

quiz.q: What can you use as a quench tank in a simple African workshop?
quiz.explanation: A metal bucket is safe for holding warm oil for quenching.

quiz.q: Why is it important to normalize or anneal a tool before hardening?
options: A) To make it softer for shaping
quiz.explanation: Annealing softens the steel, making it easier to file, grind, or drill before hardening.
